AbstractText.Label: Context
AbstractText.content: Cushing disease (CD) due to adrenocorticotropic hormone-secreting pituitary tumors can be a management challenge.

AbstractText.Label: Objective
AbstractText.content: To better understand the outcomes of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for CD and define its role in management.

AbstractText.Label: Setting
AbstractText.content: Ten medical centers participating in the International Gamma Knife Research Foundation.

AbstractText.Label: Patients
AbstractText.content: Patients with CD with >6 months endocrine follow-up.

AbstractText.Label: Main Outcome Measures
AbstractText.content: The primary outcome was control of hypercortisolism (defined as normalization of free urinary cortisol). Radiologic response and adverse radiation effects (AREs) were recorded.

AbstractText.Label: Results
AbstractText.content: In total, 278 patients met inclusion criteria, with a mean follow-up of 5.6 years (0.5 to 20.5 years). Twenty-two patients received SRS as a primary treatment of CD. Mean margin dose was 23.7 Gy. Cumulative initial control of hypercortisolism was 80% at 10 years. Mean time to cortisol normalization was 14.5 months. Recurrences occurred in 18% with initial cortisol normalization. Overall, the rate of durable control of hypercortisolism was 64% at 10 years and 68% among patients who received SRS as a primary treatment. AREs included hypopituitarism (25%) and cranial neuropathy (3%). Visual deficits were related to treatment of tumor within the suprasellar cistern (P = 0.01), whereas both visual (P < 0.0001) and nonvisual cranial neuropathy (P = 0.02) were related to prior pituitary irradiation.

AbstractText.Label: Conclusions
AbstractText.content: SRS for CD is well tolerated and frequently results in control of hypercortisolism. However, recurrences can occur. SRS should be considered for patients with persistent hypercortisolism after pituitary surgery and as a primary treatment in those unfit for surgery. Long-term endocrine follow-up is essential after SRS.
